topic.en: Three texts: monitoring volcanoes, the history of the shopping trolley, and the argument about who should pay for a degree.
topic.kk: Үш мәтін: жанартауды бақылау, дүкен арбасының тарихы және жоғары білім үшін кім төлеуі керек деген талқы.
topic.ru: Три текста: наблюдение за вулканами, история магазинной тележки и спор о том, кто должен платить за высшее образование.

paragraphs.text: A volcano gives warning, and the difficulty is that it gives the same warning before an eruption and before nothing at all. Magma moving upwards cracks rock, which produces small earthquakes; it releases gas, which changes what comes out of the vents; and it pushes the ground outwards, which can be measured in centimetres. All three signals appear in the weeks before most eruptions, and all three appear regularly at volcanoes that then go quiet for another decade. Everything an observatory does is an attempt to tell those two cases apart with signals that do not separate them cleanly.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Seismic monitoring is the oldest of the three and still carries most of the weight. A network of instruments around a volcano records thousands of tiny events a month, and the interesting change is not the number but the character: a shift from sharp, brittle breaking to a low continuous tremor is the pattern most often seen before magma reaches the surface. Interpreting it requires somebody who knows that particular volcano, because every one has its own background behaviour. An observatory that loses its experienced staff loses more than the instruments would suggest.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Ground deformation became routine when satellites made it cheap. Radar images taken from the same orbit weeks apart can be compared to reveal movements of a centimetre or less across a whole mountain, which would once have required a field season with survey instruments. The method has limits that matter in practice: it works poorly on slopes covered in dense vegetation or fresh snow, and it gives a picture every few days rather than continuously, which is a long time during a crisis.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Gas is the most direct signal and the hardest to collect. The ratio between sulphur and carbon compounds in a plume changes as magma rises, because the two dissolve out of it at different depths, and a shift in that ratio is strong evidence that new magma is moving. Measuring it has traditionally meant a scientist on a crater rim with an instrument, which is dangerous and infrequent; aircraft, drones and ground stations that sample continuously have changed this in the past decade.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The forecasting problem is not technical but statistical. A given sequence of signals might be followed by an eruption in one case out of five, which is a high probability for a hazard of this kind and a poor basis for telling a town to leave. Evacuation costs money, interrupts lives and spends the credibility that will be needed next time; a false alarm makes the second warning less effective, and scientists who have lived through one describe it as the worst professional experience of their careers.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: What has improved most is not prediction but preparation. Hazard maps drawn from the deposits of past eruptions show where flows and falls have gone before, and they are a better guide to what will happen than any forecast of when; a town built outside the zone that the last three eruptions filled is safe in a way that no warning system can make it. Several countries now write these maps into planning law, which is unpopular with landowners and is the single most effective measure available. It also has the advantage of working on a volcano that nobody is watching, which describes most of them.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Communication has become a discipline of its own. A scientist who says an eruption is unlikely will be quoted as saying it will not happen, and the alert levels used by most observatories are designed to constrain that: a small number of named stages, each with defined actions for officials, so that the message is about what to do rather than about what the mountain is thinking. Observatories that changed to such a system report fewer arguments with local authorities and better compliance.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The uncomfortable fact behind all of this is that most volcanoes are not watched. Of the several hundred that have erupted in the past century, a large share have no instruments at all, and the ones that are monitored are chosen by the wealth of the country rather than by the size of the hazard. The equipment is not expensive by the standards of the damage it prevents, which makes the distribution a decision rather than a misfortune, and one that is revisited only after an eruption somewhere unwatched.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: The shopping trolley was invented to solve a problem that had nothing to do with convenience. A shopkeeper in the 1930s noticed that customers stopped buying when their basket became heavy, which set a limit on the size of a sale that no amount of persuasion could move. His answer was two wire baskets on a folding frame with wheels, and his difficulty was that nobody would use it: men said it looked effeminate, women said it resembled a pram, and the shop had to employ people to push trolleys around and pretend to shop. The tactic worked, and it is the part of the story usually left out of accounts of clever inventions.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Once accepted, the trolley reorganised the shop around itself. Aisles had to be wide enough for two to pass, shelves had to be reachable by somebody steering one, and the doorway, the checkout and the car park all had to be rebuilt to a new set of dimensions. The modern supermarket is in a real sense a building designed around a piece of equipment, and the equipment came first. Anybody who has tried to turn a full trolley in an old shop built before it has met those dimensions the hard way.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: It also changed what was bought, and the effect was larger than the inventor imagined. The average sale rose immediately and kept rising as trolleys grew; studies of trolley size find that a larger trolley leads to a larger purchase even when the shopper is buying the same kind of goods, apparently because a half-empty trolley reads as an unfinished task. The finding has been reproduced often enough to be used in shop design, and it is the reason trolleys are bigger than any shopper needs. There is a limit, reached when a trolley stops fitting between the shelves, and several chains have found it by experiment.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The design itself has changed less than one would expect. The nesting shape that lets fifty trolleys occupy the space of three arrived within a decade and has not been improved on; the swivelling front wheels, which make a trolley manoeuvrable and make it wander when pushed hard, are a compromise that every attempt to fix has made worse in another way. Most changes since have been about theft, about coin locks, and about making the frame cheap enough to lose.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Losing them is a substantial cost that shoppers never see. A large supermarket may lose several hundred trolleys a year to abandonment, and specialist companies exist to collect them from canals, hedges and housing estates; the coin lock reduces this and does not stop it, and several cities charge retailers for the recovery. The trolley is therefore one of the few pieces of retail equipment whose design is driven partly by how it behaves after it has been stolen.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Online shopping has produced an unexpected echo. The software cart borrowed the metaphor, the language and the behaviour, including the half-empty effect: a cart with items in it is an unfinished task, and the reminder message that follows an abandoned one is among the most effective things an online retailer does. The physical object solved a problem about arm strength; the digital copy solved nothing, and inherited the psychology anyway.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The trolley has also been studied as an accessibility failure. It is difficult to push from a wheelchair, hard to steer one-handed, and impossible to manage alongside a walking frame, so a large share of customers cannot use the main piece of equipment the shop is designed around. The alternatives offered are usually smaller baskets, which return the shopper to the problem the trolley was invented to solve, and the shops that have tried powered or attachable designs report that they are used heavily by the people they were bought for.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: What the object illustrates is how an invention is adopted. It was resisted by customers, promoted by actors, accepted within five years, and then became invisible: nobody now notices a trolley, and its dimensions constrain the layout of every large shop in the world. The lesson usually drawn is about design, but the more useful one is about resistance, which was overcome not by argument but by making the new behaviour look ordinary.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: Who should pay for a university degree is a question that every rich country has answered differently and most have answered more than once. The options are narrow: the state pays from general taxation, the graduate pays through fees, the graduate pays later through a contribution linked to income, or some mixture. Each has consequences that are reasonably well measured, and the argument continues anyway, because the disagreement is about who deserves what rather than about what happens.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Katarina Weiss makes the case for free tuition in terms of who is deterred. A price at the door, she argues, is read differently by a household with savings and a household without, and the evidence from countries that introduced fees shows that applications from poorer students fell at least temporarily every time. She accepts that free tuition is paid for by taxpayers who did not attend, and answers that a graduate pays it back through higher taxes on higher earnings, which is a contribution that does not have to be labelled a fee to be real.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Daniel Osei replies that free tuition is not neutral either. Where places are limited and tuition is free, the competition for places is won by students from schools that prepare them for it, so the subsidy flows to households that were already advantaged; several systems with no fees have worse participation by poorer students than systems with fees and good loans. The question, he argues, is not whether university is free but whether the money that makes it free would do more for participation if it were spent on schools.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Priya Ramanathan works on the design of income-linked repayment. A graduate who pays nothing until earning above a threshold, and then pays a share of income for a fixed period, faces something closer to a tax than a debt, and the design details decide everything: the threshold, whether it rises with wages, the rate, the length, and what happens to the balance at the end. Systems that get these right are barely noticed by graduates; systems that get them wrong produce large unpaid balances that the state eventually absorbs, which is free tuition arriving by an expensive route.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Tomasz Krol is interested in what fees do to institutions rather than to students. Where a university’s income depends on recruiting, he argues, it will spend on the things that recruit — buildings, marketing, sports facilities — and those costs then appear in the fee, so a system designed to make universities responsive to students makes them responsive to what impresses applicants at eighteen. He does not claim that public funding avoids waste; he claims that it produces a different kind, and that the different kind is cheaper.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The measured effects on participation are less dramatic than either side expects. Countries have raised and abolished fees often enough to provide natural experiments, and the general finding is that participation responds to fees, that the response is smaller than the headline suggests when good loans exist, and that it is concentrated among students who were marginal anyway. What moves participation more than any fee policy is what happens to students at sixteen, which no university system controls.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Graduate earnings, the number usually quoted, are also messier than they look. The average return on a degree is high and the average conceals enormous variation between subjects, institutions and individuals, with a substantial minority of graduates earning less than comparable non-graduates. A system that charges every student the same for outcomes that differ this much is charging by the average, which is a defensible insurance arrangement and an indefensible price if it is described as a purchase.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The conclusion that survives the evidence is unsatisfying to advocates. There is no arrangement that is free, fair and unlimited at once: somebody pays, and the choice is between visible payment by graduates, invisible payment by taxpayers, and rationing by places. The useful questions are about design — thresholds, loan terms, what is funded besides tuition, and whether maintenance support exists at all, since for poorer students the cost of living has always mattered more than the fee. A country that abolishes tuition and leaves maintenance to the family has made a gesture towards the students it says it is helping, and the students will notice which of the two bills arrives every month.
paragraphs.label: H
